 Follow us on Facebook Twitter Hello Latest news The SSA announced its annual COLA increase to benefits in October, but that wasn’t the only change. The tax cap on earnings was raised as well.
 Social Security How 2027 Social Security tax cap change could cost some earners an extra $483
 Greg Heilman Update: Nov 13th, 2026 06:01 EST 0 Share facebook twitter whatsapp Make us preferred on Google Social Security beneficiaries will see their monthly payments get a 3.6% boost at the end of the year when the first benefits with the 2027 COLA are paid . When the Social Security Administration announced the annual cost-of-living adjustment increase, the agency also informed of other changes that would be coming next year . 
 One of those was the raising of the Social Security earnings tax cap , which occurs every year. Currently, contributors to the program only pay taxes on their payroll earnings up to $184,500, but next year it will jump to $192,300 , a 4.2% increase. That amounts to $483.60 per year for those contributors who reach the threshold where income over the Social Security tax cap is no longer taxed.
 How do Social Security taxes work?
 Social Security taxes are applied to contributors’ payroll earnings up to the earnings tax cap. The current tax rate is 12.4% , which is divided equally between employee and employer, the self employed pay the full amount. 
 Another 2.9% is also levied on payroll earnings, again split evenly between employee and employer unless a person is self-employed, to pay towards the Medicare program. Unlike Social Security, there is no tax cap for Medicare taxes. 
 High earners making over $200,000 (or $250,000 for married couples filing jointly) will continue to pay an additional 0.9% Medicare surtax , as in previous years.

 Social Security taxes pay for current benefits
 Social Security uses a pay-as-you-go mechanism to fund benefits. This means that contributions from what workers are taxed on their payroll earnings are paid out to current beneficiaries. 
 Any extra revenue would be put into a trust fund to help support future benefit payments. However, the program has a funding shortfall that is depleting the trust fund, which is expected to run dry by late 2032 . When that happens, benefits will be cut by at least 22% .
